claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a non-equilibrium metastable solid solution containing only minor dispersed phases.
Thermal exposure can cause a metastable HEA solid solution to decompose and form intermetallic phases.
Exposure at 600–800 °C triggers segregation of Mg from the metastable matrix.
Segregated Mg forms Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates by thermally activated nucleation and growth.
The Mg-rich intermetallic compounds nucleate particularly at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates serve as heterogeneous nucleation sites that disturb formation of a continuous protective oxide layer.
Increasing the Mg-rich intermetallic volume fraction makes the oxide scale less coherent.
A less coherent oxide scale is a less effective barrier to oxidation and corrosive attack.
Service-like exposure will increase the Mg-rich intermetallic volume fraction relative to the rapidly quenched initial state.
Service-like exposure will produce a more discontinuous or less adherent oxide scale than in the initial state.
The altered oxide scale will correlate with an accelerated corrosion rate.
The altered oxide scale will correlate with higher oxidation mass gain.
Rapid quenching retains the original metastable solid-solution state with minimal intermetallic precipitation.
The rapidly quenched state has robust protective oxide-scale properties because it contains minimal intermetallic precipitation.
The proposed transformation and degradation mechanism is operative specifically between 600 °C and 800 °C in low-level oxidizing or corrosive environments.
Below 600 °C, the metastable state persists without significant intermetallic formation affecting the oxide scale.
Under inert conditions, the metastable state persists without significant intermetallic formation affecting the oxide scale.
Hours-to-days of exposure are sufficient to capture the relevant transformation kinetics.
The critical intermetallic size or volume fraction needed to compromise the oxide scale and its quantitative relationship to degradation are unknown.
